summary:
We built an interactive story website that shows how the NASA-ISRO NISAR radar satellite measured the ground movement caused by the magnitude 7.0 earthquake near Nagqu, Tibet, on 22 October 2026.

We started with a NISAR interferogram made from two passes on 19 and 31 October, which straddle the earthquake. We cleaned the data, removed the smooth background trend, and turned the radar signal into two maps: colored fringes and displacement along the satellite’s line of sight. On the site, visitors can switch between the two layers, zoom into the fault zone, and read plain explanations of earthquakes, radar and InSAR.

This answers the “Dancing with SARs” challenge by taking a hard-to-read radar product and making one type of surface change easy to see and understand. It matters because earthquakes often hit remote places where ground instruments are scarce, and radar can see through clouds and darkness. Our work is a student analysis, not an official model, and the site is open about its limits.
details:
What it does: It explains how earthquakes and NISAR work, then lets you explore the real NISAR deformation map of the Nagqu earthquake on an interactive map.

Benefits and impact: It makes satellite radar data understandable for students and the public, and shows how radar can help study earthquakes in remote areas.

Tools: Python (h5py, NumPy, rasterio, Matplotlib) to process the data, QGIS to check the maps, and HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the site, hosted on GitHub Pages. We found the data with ASF Vertex and took earthquake details from USGS.

What’s creative: We told it as a story rather than a data portal, and we paired the fringe view with a displacement view of the same event.

What we considered: The data is an early rapid-response product, we only had one viewing direction, and the 12-day pair includes aftershocks. We also kept the scope to one event so we could check it properly.

AI use: We used AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Antigravity and NotebookLM) for guidance, code help, an illustration and the slides. We ran the processing ourselves and reviewed the results.
